task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper explainer for general readers answering the question: Why is semiconductor manufacturing so concentrated geographically, and why is it so hard to build new chip factories? Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of March 25, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Semiconductor chips are produced in fabrication plants called fabs; the most advanced fabs manufacture transistors with features measured in nanometers — a nanometer is one-billionth of a meter, roughly 10 atomic diameters.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and Samsung together manufacture the vast majority of the world's most advanced chips; TSMC alone produces about 90% of chips below 5 nanometers.
Building a leading-edge fab costs $15 to $25 billion and takes three to five years to construct and commission; the equipment inside the fab is also extraordinarily specialized.

Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines, used to print the smallest chip features, are produced by only one company in the world — ASML of the Netherlands; each machine costs approximately $200 million and weighs 180 tonnes.

Chip manufacturing requires ultra-pure chemicals (with parts-per-trillion purity), ultra-pure water, vibration-controlled floors, and Class 1 cleanrooms — air cleaner than any hospital operating room.

Semiconductor engineer Dr. James Ren of Pacific Technology Institute said: "A leading-edge fab is not a building that makes things. It is a precision instrument at the scale of a city block. It cannot simply be moved or replicated by following a recipe."

The geographic concentration of chip manufacturing in Taiwan creates a systemic risk for global supply chains; any disruption — military, seismic, or operational — would affect the supply of chips used in electronics, vehicles, medical devices, and defense systems.
The U.S. CHIPS and Science Act, passed in 2022, allocated $52 billion to incentivize semiconductor manufacturing in the United States; several companies announced new fab projects using the funding.

Building a fab workforce requires years of specialized training; TSMC reported challenges finding enough qualified technicians for its Arizona fab and extended the training period to bring workers up to its standards.
Chip manufacturing depends on global supply chains for raw materials: gallium, germanium, neon gas (used in lasers), and dozens of specialized chemicals; no single country produces all of them.
Taiwan's geography — near the Pacific Ring of Fire — creates seismic risk, though TSMC fabs are engineered with seismic isolation systems and have maintained operations through major earthquakes.
Water is a major input: a large fab uses 10 to 20 million liters of ultra-pure water per day; siting in arid regions requires substantial water infrastructure.
Fab electricity consumption is also large: a leading-edge fab draws 150 to 300 megawatts, equivalent to a small city; the fab industry is a significant consumer of industrial electricity.
Dr. Ren said the tacit knowledge embedded in a chip factory's operations — the accumulated expertise of thousands of engineers — takes a decade or more to develop and cannot be transferred quickly.

The international chip supply chain is highly interdependent: a chip designed in the U.S. may be manufactured in Taiwan using Dutch lithography machines, Japanese chemicals, and South Korean memory, then assembled in Malaysia.
Export controls on advanced chip manufacturing equipment — imposed by the U.S., Netherlands, and Japan starting in 2022–2023 — limit China's access to EUV machines and some deposition equipment.

Chip manufacturing is subject to Moore's Law, the observation that transistor density doubles roughly every two years; staying on this trajectory requires continuous reinvestment in new equipment and processes.

Dr. Ren said the U.S. CHIPS Act investments address the capital cost but not the workforce and supply chain challenges; the U.S. will depend on imported chemicals and equipment for any new domestic fabs.

A mature-node fab — producing chips at 28 nanometers or larger, used in automobiles and industrial equipment — costs $3 to $5 billion and is more broadly buildable; the 2021 chip shortage affected these nodes as much as leading-edge ones.

China is investing heavily in domestic semiconductor manufacturing; it can produce 28-nanometer chips domestically but remains unable to produce chips below 7 nanometers without foreign equipment it is now restricted from purchasing.

forbidden_additions: a market share figure for TSMC different from 90% of sub-5nm chips
an EUV machine price different from $200 million
a claim that China can produce chips below 7 nanometers domestically
